content:
A salaried position, a scholarship and a self-funded place can lead to very different doctoral experiences. Compare the actual contract and funding offer rather than assuming every PhD in a country follows the same model.

The three systems on the same 2026 figures

Money first, because it is the easiest to compare wrongly. The UK pays a tax-free stipend — £21,805 from 1 October 2026, £23,805 in London — with fees normally paid by the funder, but most international applicants compete for a small share of studentships open to any fee status. Germany employs its doctoral candidates: 65 per cent of TV-L E13 step 1 pays €3,094 gross (≈€2,180 net) with pension and social insurance, and no tuition. The Netherlands employs too: the cao NU scale from July 2026 runs €3,204 to €4,051 across four years plus 8 per cent holiday allowance and an 8.3 per cent year-end bonus. On gross income the Dutch model wins; on take-home in a cheap German city, Germany often wins; on fee-free access for the self-funded, Germany and the Netherlands beat the UK outright.

Everything else follows the employment model. Duration: UK 3-4 years, Germany 3-4 (with the Wissenschaftszeitgesetz capping fixed-term research employment), Netherlands 4 years with a formal go/no-go. Language: UK and Dutch programmes run in English throughout; German doctoral work runs in English in the sciences but admin and daily life reward German. Structure: the UK has the most taught-doctorate infrastructure (CDTs, 1+3 routes), Germany the most individual- apprenticeship-style supervision, the Netherlands the most formalised mid-term evaluation. The table is the summary; your supervisor's style is the deciding variable the table cannot hold.

[[chart:three-income]][[chart:three-total]]Compare the offer, not a national stereotype

The UK, Germany and the Netherlands each have different doctoral routes. Universities within the same country can offer different contracts, funding packages and training structures. Read the vacancy and award terms before deciding what the country's usual model means for you.

In the UK, a studentship commonly combines tuition support and a maintenance stipend. Check whether it covers your fee status and the full expected research period. Admission to a PhD and selection for a studentship may be separate decisions.

In Germany, a doctorate may be supported through university or research-institute employment, a scholarship or external funding. For employment, check the pay agreement, contract percentage and duration. A part-time contract percentage changes the gross payment even if the pay group is the same.

In the Netherlands, many advertised doctoral roles use employment contracts. Scholarship-funded and externally funded candidates also exist. Ask which route applies, which agreement governs an employment offer and whether registration or other costs are covered.

Ask the same questions in all three countries

  • What research question would you work on, and who supervises it?
  • What payment and tuition support are guaranteed in writing?
  • Is the payment a gross salary, a net amount or a stipend?
  • How long does funding last, and what happens if the project runs longer?
  • Are teaching, lab support or other duties part of the role?
  • What would housing and insurance cost in the specific city?

Consider how you want to work

A structured doctoral programme may include courses, rotations and cohort training. An individually arranged project may offer a different degree of flexibility. Neither format automatically provides better supervision. Look at the group's actual practices and ask current researchers about support, expectations and access to facilities.

Language can affect daily life and professional opportunities even when the research is conducted in English. Immigration conditions and options after graduation also depend on your circumstances and the rules in force when you apply.

Use research fit, reliable funding and workable living conditions as your comparison criteria. The suitable choice is the offer that supports the work you want to do and the commitments you need to manage.

Compare the same research period

If one offer funds three years and another four, calculate the guaranteed support over each appointment rather than comparing one month alone. Check whether tuition, insurance or research costs are covered separately. For an employment contract, ask about duties, paid leave and recognised experience. For a scholarship, read renewal and outside-work conditions. Also compare what happens if the research takes longer than planned. These questions expose differences that a country-level salary table can hide, particularly when a stipend and an employee salary use different deductions and benefits.

Start with three real offers or vacancies

A useful comparison begins with a specific project in each country. Read the proposed research, supervisor information and financial conditions before looking at a country's reputation. Two laboratories in the same city can offer very different supervision, equipment and expectations. A national comparison can organise questions, but it cannot identify the right research environment on its own.

Choose three criteria that matter to your situation. For example, you might need a particular experimental platform, reliable support for the whole research period and accommodation suitable for a family. Give those requirements priority before comparing optional benefits. A prestigious project that lacks a resource essential to your question is not automatically the stronger research choice.

Compare the arrangements side by side

QuestionWhat to compare across all three destinations
Research scopeAdvertised question, freedom to adjust it and expected contribution.
SupervisionMeeting pattern, co-supervision and support when the project stalls.
MoneySpendable income, fee coverage, guaranteed period and startup costs.
DutiesTeaching, project deliverables, training and time for the thesis.
ResourcesConfirmed access to equipment, data, participants and computing.
Practical lifeHousing, language needs, household costs and relevant residence conditions.

Ask current researchers about ordinary working practices rather than asking only whether they like the university. How are experiments reviewed? What happens if equipment fails? How are authorship and collaboration discussed? Their experience can help you form questions, while the contract and university policies remain the place to verify formal commitments.

Look at training and independence together

A taught or cohort-based first stage can be useful if you need methodological training or want to explore several groups. An individually arranged project can offer a different kind of focus. Neither structure removes the need for good supervision. Read the actual programme requirements and ask how the first year leads into a feasible thesis plan.

For an advertised project, identify which parts are already fixed by the grant and where the researcher can shape the work. For a self-proposed topic, ask whether the supervisor and resources are confirmed. A broad promise of academic freedom is less useful than knowing what can be changed without undermining funding or feasibility.

Make a decision you can explain

Write a short paragraph for each option: the question you would study, why you are prepared for it, the support available and the unresolved issue. Then compare the paragraphs against your initial criteria. This exposes missing evidence without pretending that a numerical score can measure every aspect of a doctorate.

Is a salaried doctorate always better than a studentship?

No universal ranking follows from the payment label. Compare net income, covered costs, benefits, duties and research support. A well-funded studentship and an employment contract can each be workable under different arrangements.

Should post-study residence decide the country?

It can be one relevant constraint, but check current official eligibility separately. A doctoral offer does not guarantee later employment, sponsorship or settlement, and future rules should not be treated as fixed.

Questions applicants often ask

Which is better for a PhD: UK, Germany or the Netherlands?

On money: the Netherlands pays the most (€3,204-4,051 gross plus allowances), Germany's E13 contracts follow, and UK stipends are lowest but tax-free with fees paid. On structure: the UK offers the most taught-doctorate support, Germany the most individual supervision, the Netherlands the most formalised progression. Match the model to how you work.

Do I need the local language for a PhD in Germany or the Netherlands?

For the doctorate itself, no — Dutch programmes run in English and German doctoral work does too in the sciences. For daily life and the German settlement fast-track (B1 German unlocks the two-year PR route for graduates), the local language is a practical and financial advantage.
